sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Jagannātha** (*jagannatha*) — Lord of the World, Puri, Devotion · Lord of the universe — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Lord of the World, Puri, Devotion". The name means "Lord of the universe"[^1].

**Jagannātha** belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is associated with lord of the world, puri, devotion.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Jagannātha** and serves its temple at [jagannatha.com](https://punicodex.com/jagannatha/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *jagannatha* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Devanagari as **जगन्नाथ**. Etymologically it means "Lord of the universe"[^1].

Sanskrit Jagannātha, from jagat 'world, universe' + nātha 'lord, protector'; the form of Krishna worshipped at Puri.

The ASCII form *jagannatha* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Jagannātha** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **j** → **J** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **g** → **g** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **a** → **ā** — Macron: long vowel
- **t** → **t** — Same
- **h** → **h** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

The canonical temple for this name is served at **jagannatha.com**[^2].

sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/jagannatha/** — Sanskrit Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **J** — Initial character of the restored form Jagannātha.
- **agannātha** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Sanskrit tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'JAGANNATHA' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Sanskrit** — Jagannātha, the restored Unicode form of the name

Jagannātha is Tier 1 because the Sanskrit form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

sections.body:

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Jagannātha is written in Devanagari as जगन्नाथ
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The stories of **Jagannātha** circulate within the Sanskrit corpus, where the figure embodies lord of the world, puri, devotion.[^1]

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Jagannātha is attested in the canonical Sanskrit sources as a figure associated with lord of the world, puri, devotion.[^2]

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "Lord of the universe" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Jagannātha**, "Lord of the World," is a form of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa worshipped at the great temple in Purī, Odisha. He appears with his siblings Balabhadra and Subhadrā in the famous Rathayātrā festival, when enormous chariots carry the deities through the city.[^1] The cult integrates Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, tribal, and tantric elements. The annual Rathayātrā attracts millions of pilgrims, who consider touching the ropes of the god's chariot a supreme spiritual blessing.[^2]

sources.citation: Rāmāyaṇa, Vālmīki; translated by Hari Prasad Shastri, 500 BCE.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Jagannātha appears within the Sanskrit tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.[^1]

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[daksa|Dakṣa]], [[dhatr|Dhātṛ]], [[durga|Durgā]], [[ganesha|Gaṇeśa]], and [[ganga|Gaṅgā]].

sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Jagannātha continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Sanskrit tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes.[^1] The English word "juggernaut" derives from the massive Jagannātha chariot, symbolizing unstoppable force.[^1]

sections.label: Vedic References
sections.body:
Jagannātha as a regional deity is not named in the Vedas, but the Vedic ideal of the **Puruṣa** and the cosmic sacrifice underlies the Purī temple's rituals, especially the annual **Ratha Yātrā** chariot festival.[^1] Vedic fire sacrifices continue in the temple's daily *homa* rituals.[^2]

The deity is thus anchored in Vedic sacrifice even while expressed through regional Odia culture.
sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Upaniṣads
sections.body:
The **Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad** and **Chāndogya Upaniṣad** supply the Vedāntic framework in which Jagannātha is identified with Brahman, the ground of all being.[^1] Later temple theology equates the wooden images of Jagannātha, Balabhadra, and Subhadrā with the three guṇas.[^2]

The Upaniṣadic equation of ātman and Brahman underlies devotional surrender at Purī.
sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Purāṇas
sections.body:
The **Skanda Purāṇa** contains the **Purī Māhātmya**, the foundational text for Jagannātha's sacred geography and temple origins.[^1] The **Bhāgavata Purāṇa** provides the Kṛṣṇa theology that identifies Jagannātha with Kṛṣṇa, while local chronicles such as the **Mādalāpāñjī** record royal patronage.[^2]

These Purāṇic and regional sources together authorise the temple's immense ritual calendar.
sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Mantras & Stotras
sections.body:
The **Jagannātha Gāyatrī** and **Jagannātha Aṣṭaka** are central to Odia devotional practice, sung during the Ratha Yātrā and daily *āratī*.[^1] Tantric texts used in the temple prescribe **Dāru-devatā** mantras that consecrate the wooden images as living deities.[^2]

Sound is the medium through which the carved logs become the Lord of the Universe.

sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Jagannātha embodies lord of the world, puri, devotion in the Sanskrit imagination. The name's restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make the figure recognizable in the source tradition.[^1]
